claims.text: A model incorporating defect scattering and oxygen impurity effects will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical approaches.
The accuracy advantage will apply in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The relevant sample states are near-defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed multiscale approach couples first-principles electronic-structure calculations with defect and impurity scattering models and thermal-disorder effects.
Defect scattering dominates low-temperature conduction in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering and oxygen-induced impurity effects are significant over 300–1200 K.
Point defects and oxygen produce local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The defect- and oxygen-induced lattice distortions modify electron-scattering rates relative to an ideal defect-free lattice.
Perfect-crystal approaches omit additional electron scattering caused by realistic defects and impurities.
Accounting for additional defect and impurity scattering will lower or otherwise alter predicted conductivity.
Reduced phonon activity at low temperature makes defect scattering a key conductivity mechanism.
At high temperatures, both phonon and impurity scattering become dominant.
The integrated model will predict conductivity deviations of roughly 10–20% from perfect-crystal model predictions.
Intrinsic defects will slightly reduce low-temperature conductivity in nominally pristine samples.
The 1 wt.% oxygen sample will exhibit non-monotonic high-temperature conductivity because of enhanced oxygen-impurity scattering.
Conventional perfect-crystal analytical predictions typically overestimate conductivity, especially for oxygen-containing samples.
The proposed model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 1200 K and at oxygen concentrations up to about 1 wt.%.
The model may not remain accurate above 1200 K or above about 1 wt.% oxygen.
The hypothesis is falsified if the integrated model is not approximately 10% closer to measured conductivity than the perfect-crystal model across one or both temperature regimes.

contradictions.description: The nominally pristine state is described as near defect-free, but its predicted conductivity reduction is attributed to intrinsic defects. This can be reconciled only if 'near defect-free' permits a specified residual defect population.
The evaluated regimes omit 200–300 K, whereas the boundary claims applicability continuously over 0–1200 K.
